newsitem.title: POLAND: Market welcomes free Polish fuel prices, sees rise.
newsitem.headline: Market welcomes free Polish fuel prices, sees rise.

text.p: Poland fully liberalised fuel prices on Thursday and the oil sector welcomed the decision, saying it paved the way to higher profits and market coherence.

The finance ministry announced it was freeing prices of fuels and removing all administrative limits on profit margins applied to engine fuel trade in leaded and unleaded petrol as well as diesel fuel as of February 13.
"The ministry's decision will have a positive influence on the market -- it will organise it and make it profitable," said Marian Sewerski, deputy president of the Polish unit of Texaco.
Poland's biggest refinery, Plock, promptly said it would increase its prices for all types of fuel but was still analysing the scope of the rise.
The second biggest, Gdansk refinery, said it would raise its prices as of February 14 by between eight and 11 groszes (around three cents), or five to 8.5 percent.

In yet another liberalisation of the market, the finance ministry ended a requirement that producers and distributors of fuel had to inform tax offices in advance of price rises, which could then be held up for three months.
"Retail fuel prices are likely to rise by some eight to 10 groszes per litre soon," said Andrzej Szczesniak, head of the Polish Liquid Fuel Chamber grouping distributors and importers.
Maximum prices of domestically produced-fuel and distributors' profit margins on both imported and domestic fuel have so far been controlled by the finance ministry.

It had long been reluctant to free them, fearing the strong inflationary impulse such a move could cause, even though the decision was the key to the lagging restructuring and privatisation of the oil sector.

As a result of the administrative controls Polish refineries suffered reduced profits because they could not offset the rising world crude prices by increasing domestic market prices -- held down by the ministry.

The net profit of Plock halved in 1996 to about 230 million zlotys ($75.8 million) s while the net profit of the Gdansk refinery, the second biggest, fell by about 35 percent from 125 million zlotys in 1995.
Both refineries are undergoing multi-million-dollar modernisation programmes and had argued that last year's reduced profits could endanger their implementation.

"The rises will not compensate for the losses which we have suffered over the last months, and will not provide sufficient funds for the necessary modernisation of the refinery, Gdansk's financial head Stanislaw Pokojski said.
Industry officials stressed, however, that the freeing of prices would also spark fierce competition on the market.

"We will certainly not plunge into any actions which would mean a marked rise in prices, we will try to be attractive on price," said Andrzej Magrys, director of sales and logistics at Statoil Polska.

"The rises are likely to be spread over time because every firm will watch their competition on the market and if anyone raises his prices too much, others will immediately offer lower ones," said Texaco's Sewerski. ($ = 3.034 Polish Zloty)
